book: 186 - Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry

chapters.relation: The editor's Introduction explains why Spider-Man merits a philosophy book: Peter Parker is a self-reflective underdog with a strong moral compass he sometimes fails to follow, so his stories raise lived ethical questions rather than abstract metaphysics. Citing Plato's definition of philosophy as the love of wisdom and a way of life, Sanford frames the whole volume around Socrates' question 'how are you going to live your life?' and lists the questions Peter's life poses: the good life, the obligations attached to talents, friendship, identity over time, the ethics of enhancement, and whether life has meaning.

Mussett asks whether Peter Parker's painful life counts as a good life by testing five philosophers' answers against the comics and films. Kurtz's secular humanism finds Peter wanting in pleasure and acclaim (Uncle Ben dead by his inaction, J. Jonah Jameson's smear campaigns), while Rand's Objectivism condemns Spider-Man as the embodiment of the 'morality of sacrifice' she rejected, noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion. Epictetus scores Peter highly on duty but fails him on self-mastery, since his happiness hinges on attachments to Aunt May and MJ he cannot control; Frankl would see Peter's meaning in his irreplaceable responsibility, evidenced by his refusal of Dr. Judas Traveller's offer of a peaceful life at the cost of innocents (Amazing Spider-Man #402); and Aquinas vindicates Peter's suffering as good pain in a virtuous, charitable life.

Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.

White analyzes Spider-Man's public unmasking in Civil War as a familiar ethical choice between the right and the good. Peter's promise to Tony Stark and obedience to the Superhuman Registration Act are deontological duties, explicated through Kant's test of universalizing the maxim of promise-breaking, while his worry for Aunt May and MJ pulls him toward consequentialist reasoning whose uncertainty, complexity, and incommensurability the chapter details. Aunt May's 'some things are worth the risk' speech tips Peter toward principle, but the Kingpin's sniper shoots her anyway, and Peter's hellish aftermath — ending in the Mephisto deal of 'One More Day' — shows both the tragedy of doing the right thing and the argument that when consequences are unknowable one should simply do what is right.

Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.

Keeping asks what grounds the claim that great power brings great responsibility and answers through Good Samaritan ethics. Building on MacIntyre's account of human interdependence in family and community, and Mill's point that failing to aid can itself cause harm, he argues that Bad Samaritanism is a blameworthy harm-causing omission, so Spider-Man's rescues of strangers are obligatory negative duties rather than supererogatory favors. His vigilantism is excused because only he can stop supervillains, 'can implies ought' explains why his duties exceed ordinary people's, and his life-risking feats against the Sinister Six and Firelord still go beyond even what his enlarged duty demands.

Tallon uses the problem of moral luck (Williams and Nagel) to ask how blameworthy Peter really is for Uncle Ben's death: the Peter who let the thief go and the counterfactual Peter whose thief was caught at the elevator act identically, yet outcome luck makes the first feel like a murderer, clashing with Kant's Control Principle that only the good will has moral worth. Drawing on Williams's 'agent regret' and Susan Wolf's 'nameless virtue' of taking responsibility for consequences, the chapter separates culpability — Peter is guilty only of letting a thief go, with the intervening agency of the criminal breaking the causal chain — from responsibility for damage. Aunt May's own misguided confession that she caused Ben's death by arguing with him (Amazing Spider-Man #479) shows how virtuous people confuse involvement in a causal chain with guilt.

Terjesen uses spider-sense to tour early-modern philosophy of perception: against direct realism, Locke's indirect realism and its primary/secondary quality distinction suggest 'dangerousness' is a perceiver-relative secondary quality — bombs threaten Spider-Man but not the Hulk, and Mysterio manufactures danger-experiences — while Berkeley's idealism and Hume's phenomenalism radicalize the resulting skepticism about ever verifying sense data. The decisive clue is that spider-sense fails when Aunt May conks Peter with a vase (Amazing Spider-Man #114) and when his mentor Miles Warren becomes the Jackal: Peter does not fear those he loves. This supports Hume's sentimentalist account of moral judgment, on which vice is found not in the act but in the disapproving sentiment, moderated by Reid's common-sense reply that perception always already contains judgment — so spider-sense is a moralized judgment about what to avoid, not a Geiger counter.

Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.

Spencer gives a phenomenological account of bodily transformation in the films: with Merleau-Ponty, Peter's new body changes his world — walls become surfaces to climb — and grants motor knowledge that needs no calculation, while Norman Osborn's deliberately seized powers feed pride and Doc Ock's grief shows how transformation can sweep a weak will into vice. Virtue, on Aquinas's definition as the perfection of a power, develops only through choices and habits worked out across a whole life, so ethics is deeper than rule-following. With Levinas, the call to goodness is experienced bodily: sympathy with others' suffering draws Peter out of himself — he rushes into a burning building even when powerless in Spider-Man 2 — and the Green Goblin lives a self-contradiction by feigning deafness to it, while eros for Mary Jane both distracts from and ennobles the quest.

Novy asks whether it would be right to deliberately make a Spider-Man. Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge from Plato's Republic — that unchecked superpower breeds 'great corruptibility' — is made flesh in Doc Ock, Green Goblin, Lizard, and Morbius, while Bostrom's transhumanism supplies the movement the chapter defends. Against Fukuyama's bio-conservative worries about playing God, destroying equality, and violating a human essence, the chapter notes that Aunt May's bifocals and insulin already make her a cyborg, that Marvel grants personhood by behavior rather than biology (Kree, Skrulls, the Vision), and that the thought experiment of giving Mary Jane a painless 'super smile' shows we are at least sometimes obliged to enhance.

Southworth and Timm use the Clone Saga to teach real cloning science: molecular, therapeutic, and reproductive cloning, Dolly's 1-in-277 success rate, the impossibility of clone caskets and inherited memories — while crediting the 1970s writers for correctly making mitochondrial DNA the blood test that distinguishes Peter from Ben Reilly. They then evaluate the characters' reactions: Leon Kass's 'wisdom of repugnance,' which holds that a clone's genotype 'has already lived' and despotically fixes its life's expectations, explains Kane's genocidal self-loathing and Peter's rage and despair when told he is the clone, while Gregory Pence's rebuttal — that such repugnance rests on false expectations, as with twins or children of interracial couples — vindicates MJ's and Ben's insistence that a clone's moral worth lies in what it does, not where its genes came from.

Taliaferro and Little ask whether Spider-Man can champion justice and love Mary Jane at the same time, framed by Mandela's tension between obligations to family and to community. Through paired scenarios — rescuing an endangered coworker at possible mortal cost versus a lover's plea to become a surgeon rather than join a deadly crime-fighting unit — they conclude that justice trumps romance in unforeseen emergencies, while romance can rightly govern the choice of a vocation. For Spider-Man the two fuse rather than conflict, since MJ loves him partly for his commitment to justice, though Gwen Stacy's death on the bridge — where his webbing snapped her neck — shows a hero can lose both at once.

Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.

Robichaud argues Peter actually wronged two of his worst enemies before they became them. Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, tempered by reflective equilibrium, condemns his years-long deception of best friend Harry about being Spider-Man and about Norman's death — a silence that later explodes Harry into the second Green Goblin — and having unknowingly made the sentient alien symbiote dependent on him during Secret Wars, Peter owed it more caution than blasting it off as dirty laundry. Still, two wrongs don't make a right: Harry may 'Goblinize' only in self-defense, not revenge, and by the doctrine of double effect Spider-Man may ring the bell tower to separate Venom from Eddie Brock even foreseeing the symbiote's destruction and Eddie's breakdown; finally, his special obligations oblige him to seek his friends' reform, not merely their capture.

Malloy asks why Spider-Man jokes while fighting for his life. After surveying the superiority theory (Plato, Hobbes's 'sudden glory'), Kant's incongruity theory, and Freud's relief theory, he adapts F. H. Buckley's moral-superiority account: Spidey's quips at the Vulture's boasting, Doc Ock's mercilessness, Kingpin's girth, and J. Jonah Jameson's sourness are moral corrections meant to goad their butts toward the virtues they lack. Aristotle's buffoon/wit distinction saves Spidey from vulgarity — he can be serious after Gwen Stacy's death — and his teasing of allies like the Thing and Captain America teaches social virtues, though the jokes rarely reform anyone.

White examines the fan fury over 'One More Day,' in which Peter and MJ trade their marriage to Mephisto to save Aunt May's life. Virtue ethics evaluates people by stable character traits, but situationist psychology (the pay-phone coin experiments, Doris's Lack of Character) argues behavior tracks trivial situational details, not traits — while fictional characters like Captain America and Peter Parker are written with simpler, firmer traits, so making a deal with the devil reads as glaringly out of character and betrays the audience's trust. Since the true agents were editor Joe Quesada and the writers, White asks whether creators owe fans fidelity to a character's established identity, and closes by arguing that even if real character is situational, integrity — being the same person across situations — remains a virtue worth aspiring to, including toward ourselves.

Sanford argues, through the arc of the Raimi trilogy, that Peter becomes good by becoming the narrator of his own life. On Aristotle's Poetics — a story has a beginning, middle, and end, and art imitates life — and MacIntyre's claim that man is a 'story-telling animal' whose life is 'the unity of a narrative quest,' Peter's involuntary obligations (orphanhood, Uncle Ben's death, the spider bite, love for MJ) ground the voluntary ones, and his quest is to use his great powers responsibly. Tracking Aristotle's categories, Peter moves from incontinence (vengeance on Flint Marko, the jazz-club strut in Spider-Man 3) through continence to genuine virtue, and his practice of telling his own story — 'it's the choices that make us who we are' — models how we must get our own stories straight to flourish.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century novelist-philosopher whose Objectivism holds rational self-interest and voluntary trade, not sacrifice, as the moral ideal.
holes.why: Chapter 9 gives Objectivism a full section, arguing Spider-Man personifies the 'morality of sacrifice' Rand condemned and noting Steve Ditko's Objectivist devotion.

holes.name: Paul Kurtz
holes.what: Secular humanist philosopher who defined the good life as happiness through self-realization plus benevolence, fairness, and love, without religion.
holes.why: Chapter 9 opens with Kurtz's secular-humanist test of whether Peter Parker's life of enterprise, friendship, and hardship counts as happy.

holes.name: The Bad and the True Infinite
holes.what: Hegel's distinction between a 'bad infinity' of endless, never-completed progression and the 'true infinite' that is complete and self-related like a circle.
holes.why: Chapter 10 frames Peter's endless, unsatisfiable obligation as Hegel's bad infinity and contrasts it with the self-sufficient ethics of the true infinite.

holes.name: Supererogation
holes.what: Acts that are praiseworthy to perform but not blameworthy to omit — beyond the call of duty.
holes.why: Chapter 14 hinges on whether Spider-Man's rescues are obligatory duties or supererogatory acts, concluding failing to aid is a harm-causing omission and thus required.

holes.name: Transhumanism (human enhancement)
holes.what: The movement advocating the use of technology to expand human physical and cognitive capacities beyond biological limits.
holes.why: Chapter 21's entire argument defends the ethics of making a Spider-Man against bio-conservative objections about playing God, equality, and human essence.

holes.name: Leon Kass
holes.what: Bioethicist whose 'wisdom of repugnance' holds cloning wrong because a clone's genotype 'has already lived,' despotically fixing the clone's life to another's expectations.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Kass's argument to explain Kane's self-loathing and Peter's despair at learning he may be the clone.

holes.name: Gregory Pence
holes.what: Bioethicist who defends cloning, arguing repugnance toward clones rests on false expectations, like prejudices against twins or mixed-race children.
holes.why: Chapter 22 uses Pence's rebuttal of Kass to vindicate MJ's and Ben's view that a clone's worth comes from its actions, not its genes.
